batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::05 Modules and Linking

cards.front: What is the source file that declares a module and all its properties?
cards.extra: Placed in the project's source root, e.g. src/main/java, so tools pick it up. It compiles to module-info.class, the module descriptor, which goes at the JAR root.

cards.front: Which four directives make up the body of a typical module declaration?
cards.extra: requires lists dependencies by module name, exports names packages that form the public API, uses names service types consumed, provides ... with ... names service implementations offered.

cards.front: By default, which types in a module's packages can code outside the module use?
cards.extra: A module has a real boundary the compiler and JVM enforce. To expose a type you must export or open the package that contains it.

cards.front: What is the effect of exports versus opens on a package?
cards.extra: Exports make the package part of the public API. Opens leaves it invisible to the compiler but lets reflection reach private members. A package may be both.

cards.front: What does requires transitive express?
cards.back: A dependency that is part of the module's own API
cards.extra: Any module reading this module automatically reads the required one. Needed when a public signature exposes types from the dependency, as java.sql does with java.xml.

cards.front: What is a modular JAR?
cards.extra: Without the descriptor it is a plain JAR. On the module path a modular JAR becomes a module; on the class path it still merges into the unnamed module.

cards.front: What is the module path, and what does it do to plain JARs?
cards.back: A list of artifacts; plain JARs become automatic modules
cards.extra: It parallels the class path but makes every artifact on it a module, enabling incremental modularisation. javac and java both understand it.

cards.front: Does a JAR having a module descriptor decide whether it is treated as a module?
cards.back: No - the path it is placed on decides
cards.extra: All JARs on the class path form the single unnamed module; all JARs on the module path become modules. So the project owner, not the dependency's maintainer, decides what is an individual module.

cards.front: How does module resolution work?
cards.back: Start at the initial module, follow each requires, error if one is missing
cards.extra: Repeat until nothing new is found; observe it with --show-module-resolution. The result is the module graph, whose edges are readability relations.

cards.front: Which module is the base module, and must you requires it?
cards.back: java.base - it is required implicitly, no clause needed
cards.extra: It holds Class, ClassLoader, java.lang, java.util and the module system itself. Resolution bootstraps it first, before any other module.

cards.front: Which three conditions must hold for module A to use a type from module B?
cards.back: Type is public, package is exported, A reads B
cards.extra: That third condition is the new part compared with plain JARs. Reading normally comes from requires, but --add-reads can add it at launch.

cards.front: Which two reliable-configuration errors does the module system detect at launch?
cards.extra: There is no notion of version beyond a string, so two versions of one module are a duplicate and rejected. A package living in two modules is a split package, also rejected. Static dependency cycles are the third check.

cards.front: What is a static dependency cycle between modules?
cards.extra: Cycles are fine at runtime, e.g. Spring reflecting over code that uses Spring annotations, but the modules must not require each other to compile. The module system rejects static cycles.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::05 Modules and Linking

cards.front: Which rule summarises which JDK namespaces are safe to use?
cards.extra: In sun.* only sun.misc and sun.reflect are exempt, exported by jdk.unsupported. In com.sun.* roughly 90% is internal and the exported remainder belongs to jdk.* modules.

cards.front: Which module exports sun.misc and sun.reflect, and why?
cards.back: jdk.unsupported - they are needed with no feasible replacement
cards.extra: Chiefly for sun.misc.Unsafe. These are the deliberate exceptions: the rest of sun.* is internal and inaccessible.

cards.front: What proportion of com.sun.* packages is internal?
cards.extra: The namespace is JDK-specific rather than standard. Roughly a tenth is exported by jdk.* modules and supported, evolving with compatibility in mind, so each usage warrants a look.

cards.front: What happens to non-exported internal types when a module is on the module path?
cards.extra: E.g. sun.util.BuddhistCalendar lives in java.base which does not export sun.util. Both the compile error and the reflective runtime exception point at strong encapsulation.

cards.front: Which JDK release changed --illegal-access default from permit to deny?
cards.extra: JDK 9 to 15 permitted deep reflective access from the class path by default. JDK 16 flipped the default, and JDK 17 removed the option entirely.

cards.front: From JDK 17 onwards, which options allow access to internal APIs?
cards.extra: Nothing else works: illegal-access is gone. Both act per module/package pair and must be supplied at launch, by whoever runs the application.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::05 Modules and Linking

cards.front: What is the syntax of --add-exports?
cards.extra: E.g. --add-exports java.base/sun.util=ALL-UNNAMED. The space can be an equals sign to suit build tools such as Maven.

cards.front: What is ALL-UNNAMED in --add-exports or --add-opens?
cards.extra: Use it while your project is not modularised. Once your code runs as a module you can name that module and expose internals to it alone.

cards.front: Which kinds of member does --add-exports expose in the target package?
cards.extra: Same visibility as a real exports: the compiler can resolve the package and code can call public API in it. Non-public types remain out of reach.

cards.front: Which kinds of member does --add-opens expose?
cards.back: All types and members, public or not, via reflection
cards.extra: It works like an opens directive applied at launch. Compilation gains nothing, so code must reach the classes reflectively, usually with setAccessible(true).

cards.front: Is --add-exports needed at compile time, at run time, or both?
cards.back: Both - repeat it on java after using it on javac
cards.extra: Compiling against an internal package only grants compile access. Launching on JDK 17+ without the flag fails again at runtime.

cards.front: What happens if you pass --add-opens to javac?
cards.back: A warning: it has no effect at compile time
cards.extra: It is a pure runtime concept bound to reflection, so javac does not reject the option. It merely reports that nothing will happen, which helps when one option string is fed to several tools.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::05 Modules and Linking

cards.front: What does --add-modules add to module resolution?
cards.extra: Resolution starts from root modules, so adding one brings it and its transitive requires into the graph even though the initial module never mentions it.

cards.front: Which three special values does --add-modules accept?
cards.extra: ALL-DEFAULT is the set picked for class-path launches, for container apps. ALL-SYSTEM adds every system module, used by test harnesses. ALL-MODULE-PATH adds every module found on the module path.

cards.front: What does --add-reads $MODULE=$TARGETS add?
cards.back: Readability edges from one module to a comma-separated list
cards.extra: The module can then use public types in the targets' exported packages without a requires clause. ALL-UNNAMED as target lets a module read the unnamed module.

cards.front: Which tool accepts --add-modules?
cards.extra: It is a resolution-time option, so each tool that resolves modules honours it. --add-reads, by contrast, is documented for the compiler and runtime.

cards.front: Give a realistic use for --add-modules.
cards.back: Pull in an optional dependency not otherwise required
cards.extra: If a module only sometimes needs java.sql it never enters the graph on its own. Listing it in --add-modules at launch adds it, usually alongside --add-reads for readability.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::05 Modules and Linking

cards.front: Which modifier on requires gives implied readability?
cards.extra: Any module that reads the declaring module automatically reads the required one too. Written requires transitive java.xml;.

cards.front: When should you use requires transitive for module B?
cards.back: When public signatures of your API refer to B's packages
cards.extra: Otherwise every client would have to add its own requires B to compile against your API. That is a hidden dependency clients could easily miss.

cards.front: Which class exposes java.sql's dependency on java.xml through its API?
cards.extra: It maps the SQL XML type, so java.xml types appear in a public signature. Driver.getParentLogger() likewise returns a java.util.logging.Logger, hence the transitive requires on java.logging.

cards.front: Contrast: java.prefs vs java.sql on java.xml.
cards.extra: Both declare requires java.xml, but only java.sql needs it transitive, because its public API mentions java.xml types such as SQLXML.

cards.front: Should a module rely on implied readability of B if it uses B's types throughout its own code?
cards.extra: Implied readability is for types used only at the boundary to the module that grants it. Using them everywhere is a genuine dependency; declaring it documents the architecture and survives refactoring.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::05 Modules and Linking

cards.front: What are the two reasons exports is a poor fit for reflection frameworks?
cards.back: It publishes the package as API, and only public members become reachable
cards.extra: Frameworks touch non-public types, constructors, accessors and fields. And exporting a package that handles HTTP requests or database access wrongly advertises it as a stable contract.

cards.front: How does opens differ from exports at compile time?
cards.back: The package stays fully encapsulated - outside code cannot compile against it
cards.extra: No exports means no compile-time access at all. Reflection is the only way in, which is exactly the intent: express that this package exists for a reflection-based framework.

cards.front: How does opens differ from exports with respect to non-public members?
cards.extra: For non-public members reflection still needs setAccessible(true). The point of opens is that the module has authorised the deep access, so no exception is thrown.

cards.front: How do you open every package of a module at once?
cards.extra: An open module behaves as if each package had its own opens. There is no wildcard form, so this keyword is the equivalent of opens com.example.*.

cards.front: In an open module, what happens to an explicit opens directive?
cards.back: Compile error - all packages are already open
cards.extra: Writing opens p; is redundant by definition, so the compiler rejects it. exports directives are still allowed and still mean what they say.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::05 Modules and Linking

cards.front: Which keyword qualifies exports or opens to specific modules?
cards.back: to followed by a comma-separated module list
cards.extra: E.g. exports com.example.internal to com.example.friend;. The named modules get full access; every other module sees strong encapsulation as if the directive had no effect.

cards.front: Which JDK module qualifies exports of com.sun.org.apache.xml.internal* to java.xml.crypto?
cards.extra: Six internal packages of the JAXP module are needed by XML cryptography, so they are exported to java.xml.crypto and nothing else. A textbook case of controlled sharing inside the JDK.

cards.front: Can a package appear in both exports p and exports p to M?
cards.extra: The plain exports already grants everyone access, which makes the qualified one pointless. The module system treats this contradiction as an implementation error.

cards.front: What does javac report when a qualified export names a module that cannot be found?
cards.extra: The target is mentioned but not required, so it may simply not be on the path at compile time. Failing the build would break builds for optional targets.

cards.front: Who must change when a new module needs access to a qualified-exported package?
cards.back: The exporting module - it must add the new target
cards.extra: That control is the feature's point: the owner decides who shares. It is also its cost, since every new friend forces an edit to the exporting module's declaration.

cards.front: Why is the use case for qualified opens much smaller than for qualified exports?
cards.back: Open targets are frameworks that won't start depending on you
cards.extra: A framework never develops a compile dependency on a package it reflects over, so unqualified opens risk little. Qualified opens add fragility when API and implementation split, such as JPA and Hibernate.

cards.front: Why can qualified opens force you to mention an implementation in your code?
cards.back: Reflection needs opening to the module that actually reflects
cards.extra: Until frameworks adopt Lookup/VarHandle forwarding, JPA plus Hibernate means opening entity packages to the Hibernate module, not the JPA module. That leaks an implementation detail into the declaration.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::05 Modules and Linking

cards.front: What does requires static demand at compile time?
cards.back: The module must be present, and is readable
cards.extra: Identical to a normal requires during compilation, so you can freely use its types in source. Absence is a compile error.

cards.front: What does requires static allow at run time?
cards.back: The module may be absent, with no error or warning
cards.extra: If it is present on the graph the requiring module reads it. If not, you simply must not reach its types, or you get a NoClassDefFoundError.

cards.front: During resolution, does the module system try to find a requires static target?
cards.back: No - it is ignored, never pulled into the graph
cards.extra: Even a matching module on the module path is not added just for the optional dependency. It enters only via another module's regular requires or via --add-modules.

cards.front: What error do you get when code touches an absent optional dependency at runtime?
cards.extra: The type check fails while loading. With a normal requires the launch would have failed early; opting out of that check means the failure can surface late instead.

cards.front: Which API tells you at runtime whether a module is present?
cards.extra: Map it to a boolean and branch before calling into the optional dependency. A library cannot check for you; the decision belongs to the code that knows whether the feature is in use.

cards.front: When can you skip the presence check for an optional dependency?
cards.back: When the only callers already need that dependency
cards.extra: A JDBC helper inside a library is reached only from code that already uses java.sql, so java.sql is guaranteed in the graph. No check is needed there.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::05 Modules and Linking

cards.front: Which class acts as the central service registry in Java?
cards.extra: It implements the service locator pattern. Call ServiceLoader.load(Service.class) to get a ServiceLoader that yields every provided implementation.

cards.front: Which two directives express the consumer and provider side of a service?
cards.extra: The consumer names the service type it will look up; the provider names which of its classes is the implementation. Services let a module call behaviour from a module it does not depend on.

cards.front: What may a provides ... with class be besides an implementor with a no-arg constructor?
cards.back: A type with a public static no-arg provider() method
cards.extra: That is the provider method form. Otherwise the provider is a concrete class extending or implementing the service with a public parameterless constructor.

cards.front: Which JDK module uses java.sql.Driver as a service of its own?
cards.extra: A module may use one of its own types as a service. It means JDBC drivers can be supplied by other modules without java.sql depending on any vendor.

cards.front: After switching to services, why can the implementation module stop exporting its package?
cards.extra: The loader instantiates providers through the descriptor, not through public API. Dropping the export shrinks the module's API surface, a bonus of the pattern.

cards.front: What is service binding during resolution?
cards.back: Resolving every module that provides a service some resolved module uses
cards.extra: It explains why simple apps resolve so many platform modules: providers are added so they are available at runtime. It is a second edge type in the module graph besides requires.

cards.front: Which JDK service lets logging frameworks receive the JDK's messages?
cards.extra: The JDK asks a LoggerFinder for Logger instances instead of writing to stdout, so a framework such as Logback can provide an implementation. Same mechanism as the JDBC Driver service.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::05 Modules and Linking

cards.front: What does the unnamed module contain?
cards.back: All classes loaded from the class path
cards.extra: Every JAR on the class path, modular or not, ends up bundled into one unnamed module. It exists so the module system can apply its rules uniformly without forcing anyone to modularise.

cards.front: What is the unnamed module's name?
cards.extra: No name means it cannot appear in a requires clause, so no explicit module can depend on class-path code. That refusal is precisely the design goal, not an oversight.

cards.front: Which other modules does the unnamed module read?
cards.back: Every module that makes it into the graph
cards.extra: It exports all its packages and opens them for reflection too. Both are the loosest settings in the module system, which is what keeps legacy class-path code working.

cards.front: A library ships a modular JAR. Does that force its users to run it as a module?
cards.back: No - a modular JAR on the class path joins the unnamed module
cards.extra: Whether a JAR is modular does not decide how it is treated; its location does. This is what lets the ecosystem modularise independently of each other.

cards.front: Code in an unnamed module prints getModule().getName(). What is the output?
cards.extra: From the module path the same call prints the module name. That contrast is the quickest way to confirm which path a JAR was launched from.

cards.front: If the initial module is the unnamed one, where does module resolution start?
cards.back: A predefined set of root modules from the runtime
cards.extra: Roughly, java.se if observable, else every java.* module exporting a package unqualified. Non-incubating runtime modules exporting unqualified packages are roots too; module-path modules never are unless --add-modules names them.

cards.front: Why does Java provide no requires class-path?
cards.back: Any class-path content would fulfil it, so it guarantees nothing
cards.extra: Reliable configuration demands that dependencies be checkable. A dependency satisfiable by any JAR is unverifiable, and two modules could disagree about where a shared library belongs.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::05 Modules and Linking

cards.front: What does jlink produce?
cards.back: A runtime image containing only the modules you picked
cards.extra: It links modules and their transitive dependencies into a JDK-like directory tree. Include your own modules and the image is a self-contained application deliverable.

cards.front: Does jlink compile bytecode to machine code?
cards.back: No - it only links, no ahead-of-time compilation
cards.extra: Your classes stay bytecode; the image just carries an OS-specific JVM plus the modules. That is why images are bound to one operating system.

cards.front: Which two options are mandatory to create an image?
cards.extra: The first names the initial modules, the second the target folder. jlink verifies that no module is missing or duplicated, then writes the image.

cards.front: How does jlink treat services by default?
cards.back: No service binding - providers must be listed
cards.extra: Deliberate, to keep images small. Add providers with --add-modules, or bind them all with --bind-services.

cards.front: Which option lists the modules that provide a given service?
cards.extra: Useful before building an image with jlink: it shows what is available in the runtime or on the module path. Then add the ones you need to --add-modules.

cards.front: Does jlink resolve optional (requires static) dependencies?
cards.extra: A static dependency would otherwise pull a module into the image only by accident. Explicitly adding it with --add-modules makes the choice deliberate.

cards.front: Can jlink link an application that depends on automatic modules?
cards.extra: An automatic module has no descriptor to link against. The app and its dependencies must be modular JARs, which is a real reason to push dependencies towards modular artefacts.

cards.front: What do you need so jlink can find your application modules?
cards.back: --module-path pointing at the folder holding them
cards.extra: Then --add-modules names the app's main module. Platform and application modules together are called the image's system modules.

cards.front: What does --launcher $NAME=$MODULE/$MAIN-CLASS generate?
cards.back: A script in the image's bin that starts that module
cards.extra: Shell script on Unix, batch file on Windows. The /$MAIN-CLASS part may be omitted if the descriptor already names a main class.

cards.front: What is the downside of launching through a jlink launcher?
cards.extra: The launcher passes them after --module, so you cannot add --add-modules ad hoc. Put options in JLINK_VM_OPTIONS or call java from the image directly.

cards.front: Does the module path on an image's launch override system modules?
cards.back: No - system modules shadow same-named module-path modules
cards.extra: A module-path entry with a system module's name is simply ignored. You can still supply extra modules, typically service providers, so users can extend the image.

cards.front: How do you generate an image for a different operating system?
cards.back: Put that OS's jmods folder on the module path
cards.extra: Run it with your own jlink; it sees foreign platform modules and links for that OS. Verify by checking for java.exe in bin, and keep JDK versions in step.
